name: Layer 2 Security
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Configure and verify port security, DHCP snooping and Dynamic ARP Inspection to stop rogue devices and spoofing at the switch.

lesson.intro: Most attacks on a LAN start with someone plugging into a wall jack. On a switch with default settings, that device can flood the MAC table, hand out fake DHCP leases, poison ARP caches to put itself in the middle of everyone's traffic, or even negotiate a trunk into every VLAN. This lesson covers the three access-edge defenses on the CCNA blueprint (port security, DHCP snooping and Dynamic ARP Inspection) in depth: you will configure each, read their show output and recover ports they shut down. It finishes with the rest of access-port hardening and 802.1X, which authenticates devices before the port opens.
objectives: Match MAC flooding, rogue DHCP, DHCP starvation, ARP poisoning and VLAN hopping to the switch feature that stops each
Configure port security with a maximum, sticky learning and a violation mode, verify it and recover an err-disabled port
Configure and verify DHCP snooping with trusted ports, option 82 settings and rate limits, and read the binding table
Configure Dynamic ARP Inspection on top of DHCP snooping, including ARP ACLs, validation checks and rate limits
Harden unused and user ports and describe 802.1X port-based authentication

sections.title: Attacks at the access edge
sections.body:
A visitor plugs a laptop into a conference room jack. With default settings, the switch puts it in the room's VLAN and starts forwarding its frames like any other host. From there, a few classic attacks are possible:

- **MAC flooding**: a tool sends thousands of frames per second, each with a different fake source MAC. The switch learns them all until its MAC address table is full. New legitimate addresses can no longer be learned, so frames to them are flooded out every port, and the attacker can capture traffic it should never see.
- **Rogue DHCP server**: the laptop answers DHCP Discovers faster than the real server and hands out leases with its own IP as the default gateway (a man in the middle) or with bogus settings (a denial of service).
- **DHCP starvation**: the attacker sends Discovers with thousands of made-up client hardware addresses until the real server's pool is empty, so real clients get nothing. It is often the first step before starting a rogue server.
- **ARP poisoning**: forged or gratuitous ARP replies claim the gateway's IP for the attacker's MAC, so hosts send their traffic to the attacker.

VLANs do not stop any of these; they all happen inside one VLAN. The defenses live on the access switch, and they share one idea, the **trust boundary**: ports facing users are untrusted and checked, while ports facing infrastructure (uplinks, routers, the real DHCP server) are trusted.
sections.code:
Attack                         Switch feature that stops it
MAC flooding                   Port security (caps MACs per port)
Unknown device on a desk port  Port security (only known or sticky MACs)
Rogue DHCP server              DHCP snooping (server messages dropped on untrusted ports)
DHCP starvation                DHCP snooping (MAC check) plus rate limiting
ARP poisoning / spoofing       Dynamic ARP Inspection (uses the snooping binding table)

activity.title: What port security limits
activity.prompt: Send frames between hosts and watch the switch learn each source MAC on the port it arrived on. Notice that the switch learns any source address it sees, with no limit and no questions asked. A MAC flooding tool abuses exactly that by inventing thousands of source MACs; port security puts a cap on how many addresses each port may teach the switch.

sections.pitfall: Assuming VLAN segmentation stops these attacks. Rogue DHCP, ARP poisoning and MAC flooding all work inside a single VLAN, which is where the attacker already is.

check.question: What does an attacker gain from a successful MAC flooding attack?
choices: The switch's administrator password
Control of the spanning tree root bridge
Frames for unlearned destinations are flooded out every port, including the attacker's
A DHCP lease with the attacker as the default gateway
check.explanation: Once the MAC table is full, the switch cannot learn real hosts' addresses and floods frames meant for them, so the attacker can capture traffic that would normally be switched only to the right port.

sections.title: Port security concepts
sections.body:
**Port security** limits which source MAC addresses, and how many, may send frames into a switch port. Each port gets a **maximum** number of secure MAC addresses (default **1**). When a frame arrives from a new source MAC that would push the port over its maximum, or from a MAC that is not allowed, that is a **violation**, and the switch reacts according to the violation mode.

Secure addresses come from three places:

- **Static**: you type them with `switchport port-security mac-address H.H.H`. Precise, but you must know every device's MAC.
- **Dynamic**: the switch learns them from traffic, up to the maximum. They are lost when the switch reloads.
- **Sticky**: learned like dynamic addresses but written into the running configuration as `switchport port-security mac-address sticky H.H.H`. Save the configuration and they survive a reload. Sticky gives you static-like control without collecting MAC addresses by hand.

Port security has one firm requirement: the port must be **statically** an access port or a trunk. On a port left in a dynamic mode (dynamic auto or desirable), IOS rejects `switchport port-security` with "Command rejected: ... is a dynamic port."

Two practical notes. A port with an IP phone and a PC behind it needs a maximum of at least **2**. And once a port uses port security, its learned addresses are no longer listed as dynamic in the MAC table; use `show mac address-table secure` (they show with type STATIC).
sections.code:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1        ! static: only this one MAC may use the port
 switchport mode access
 switchport port-security
 switchport port-security mac-address 0200.1111.1111
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/2        ! sticky: learn the first MAC and keep it
 switchport mode access
 switchport port-security
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/3        ! IP phone plus a PC behind it
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 switchport voice vlan 110
 switchport port-security
 switchport port-security maximum 2
sections.pitfall: Configuring the maximum, violation mode and sticky learning but forgetting the plain switchport port-security command. IOS keeps the settings, but port security stays disabled until that command is entered.

check.question: Port security is enabled on an access port with no other port-security options. How many MAC addresses may use the port?
choices: One
Two
Unlimited until a violation mode is set
As many as the VLAN allows
check.explanation: The default maximum is 1 secure MAC address. A second source MAC causes a violation, and the default action is to err-disable the port.

sections.title: Configuring and verifying port security
sections.body:
The configuration follows the same checklist every time:

1. Make the port a static access (or trunk) port: `switchport mode access`, plus `switchport access vlan` as needed.
2. Enable the feature: `switchport port-security`.
3. Optionally change the maximum: `switchport port-security maximum n`.
4. Optionally change the violation mode: `switchport port-security violation {protect | restrict | shutdown}` (shutdown is the default).
5. Optionally define addresses: `switchport port-security mac-address H.H.H` for static, or `switchport port-security mac-address sticky` to learn and keep them.

The most useful verification command is `show port-security interface`, shown below. Read these fields:

- **Port Status**: `Secure-up` means port security is on and the port is forwarding. `Secure-shutdown` means a violation err-disabled it.
- **Violation Mode**: protect, restrict or shutdown.
- **Maximum, Total, Configured and Sticky MAC Addresses**: the limit and what is in use. A sticky address counts as configured as well, because it is written into the configuration, so Sticky MAC Addresses is the field that tells you it was learned.
- **Last Source Address:Vlan**: the most recent source MAC seen, often the violator after a violation.
- **Security Violation Count**: how many violations were counted.

`show port-security` gives a one-line-per-port summary, and `show port-security address` lists every secure MAC. Sticky addresses appear in `show running-config` immediately, but they only survive a reload after `copy running-config startup-config`.

Port security is not limited to desk ports. On a trunk it can cap how many MAC addresses a downstream switch may introduce (for example `maximum 8`), and on an EtherChannel the configuration goes on the port-channel interface rather than on the member links.
sections.code:
SW1# show port-security interface GigabitEthernet0/1
Port Security              : Enabled
Port Status                : Secure-up
Violation Mode             : Shutdown
Aging Time                 : 0 mins
Aging Type                 : Absolute
SecureStatic Address Aging : Disabled
Maximum MAC Addresses      : 1
Total MAC Addresses        : 1
Configured MAC Addresses   : 1
Sticky MAC Addresses       : 1
Last Source Address:Vlan   : 0200.2222.2222:10
Security Violation Count   : 0

activity.title: Lock a port with port security
activity.prompt: Make G0/1 an access port in VLAN 10, then enable port security with a maximum of 1, sticky learning and the shutdown violation mode. Watch the order: what happens if you try to enable port security before the port is a static access port? Finish with show port-security and show running-config, and find where the sticky settings appear.

sections.pitfall: Forgetting that sticky MACs live in the running configuration. After a reload without copy running-config startup-config, the port learns from scratch, possibly from the wrong device.

check.question: show port-security interface reports Port Status: Secure-up and Security Violation Count: 0. What does that mean?
choices: The port is err-disabled and waiting for recovery
Port security is enabled and the port is forwarding with no violations counted
Port security is configured but not enabled
The port is a trunk and port security does not apply
check.explanation: Secure-up means port security is active and the port is up. A violation in shutdown mode would change the status to Secure-shutdown and increment the counter.

sections.title: Violation modes and err-disabled recovery
sections.body:
What the switch does on a violation depends on the mode, and all three modes discard the offending frames. The differences are in what else happens:

- **shutdown** (the default): the port is put in the **err-disabled** state. All traffic stops, the legitimate device included. `show interfaces status` shows `err-disabled`, `show port-security interface` shows `Secure-shutdown`, a syslog message is generated, and the violation counter goes up by one (it counts shutdowns, not frames).
- **restrict**: the port stays up and keeps forwarding for allowed MACs. Frames from violating MACs are dropped, a syslog message (and SNMP trap) is generated, and the violation counter increments for each violating frame.
- **protect**: the port stays up, violating frames are dropped silently. No log message, no counter. Secure, but miserable to troubleshoot: a user's device simply does not work and nothing says why.

An err-disabled port stays down until someone acts. First remove or fix whatever caused the violation, otherwise the port will shut again immediately. Then recover it manually with `shutdown` followed by `no shutdown` on the interface. Or let the switch recover automatically: `errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation` enables auto-recovery for port-security violations, and `errdisable recovery interval seconds` sets the wait (300 seconds by default).

To find every port the switch has shut, `show interfaces status err-disabled` lists them with the reason, such as psecure-violation, and `show errdisable recovery` shows which causes recover automatically and how long each port has left before it is brought back.
sections.code:
Mode       Discards bad frames  Log + SNMP  Counter increments   Port state
protect    Yes                  No          No                   Stays up (Secure-up)
restrict   Yes                  Yes         Yes, per frame       Stays up (Secure-up)
shutdown   Yes                  Yes         Yes, once per event  err-disabled (Secure-shutdown)

%PORT_SECURITY-2-PSECURE_VIOLATION: Security violation occurred, caused by
MAC address 0200.3333.3333 on port GigabitEthernet0/1.

SW1(config)# errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation
SW1(config)# errdisable recovery interval 120
sections.tip: If a user says their port is dead and show interfaces status says err-disabled, port security in shutdown mode is the first suspect.
sections.pitfall: Bouncing an err-disabled port with shutdown and no shutdown while the unauthorized device is still plugged in. The next frame from it triggers another violation and the port goes straight back to err-disabled.

check.question: Which violation mode keeps the port up for the allowed device, drops frames from extra MACs, and also logs the violation and increments the counter?
choices: protect
shutdown
restrict
disable
check.explanation: restrict drops the violating frames while keeping the port up, and it records the event with syslog, SNMP and the counter. protect does the same dropping silently, and shutdown err-disables the whole port.

sections.title: DHCP snooping: trust and the filtering rules
sections.body:
**DHCP snooping** stops rogue DHCP servers and limits DHCP starvation by inspecting DHCP messages as they cross the switch. It works per VLAN and divides ports into two kinds:

- **Trusted** ports face the real DHCP server or the path to it: uplinks, the router acting as a DHCP relay, the server's own port. Every DHCP message is allowed.
- **Untrusted** ports, the default for every port, face clients. Here the switch applies rules.

The rules follow from who normally sends what. Clients send DISCOVER, REQUEST, RELEASE and DECLINE; servers send OFFER, ACK and NAK.

1. A server message (OFFER, ACK, NAK) arriving on an untrusted port is always discarded. That alone kills a rogue server on a user port.
2. For DISCOVER and REQUEST, the switch checks that the source MAC in the Ethernet header matches the **client hardware address (chaddr)** inside the DHCP message. Starvation tools invent thousands of chaddr values from one laptop, so their requests fail this check.
3. For RELEASE and DECLINE, the switch checks the **binding table**: the message must arrive on the interface where that IP address was leased. An attacker on another port cannot release a victim's address in order to grab it.
4. Every lease that completes adds a **DHCP snooping binding**: client MAC, leased IP, lease time, VLAN and interface.

That binding table is the real prize. Dynamic ARP Inspection and IP Source Guard both check traffic against it, which makes DHCP snooping the foundation of access-layer security.
sections.code:
trusted                        untrusted
DHCP server --- Gi0/24 [  SW1  ] Gi0/3 --- PC1 (DHCP client)
                                 Gi0/5 --- attacker

On untrusted ports:
  OFFER, ACK, NAK        always dropped (only servers send these)
  DISCOVER, REQUEST      dropped if the frame's source MAC differs from chaddr
  RELEASE, DECLINE       dropped if they do not arrive on the binding's port

SW1# show ip dhcp snooping binding
MacAddress          IpAddress        Lease(sec)  Type           VLAN  Interface
------------------  ---------------  ----------  -------------  ----  --------------------
02:00:11:11:11:11   10.1.10.101      86110       dhcp-snooping   10   GigabitEthernet0/3
Total number of bindings: 1
sections.pitfall: Thinking DHCP snooping blocks client messages on untrusted ports. Client messages are checked and forwarded; only server messages are always dropped there.

check.question: With DHCP snooping enabled, a DHCPOFFER arrives on an untrusted access port. What does the switch do?
choices: Forwards it, because offers are needed for DHCP to work
Forwards it only if the MAC addresses match
Adds it to the binding table and forwards it
Drops it, because servers should never be on untrusted ports
check.explanation: OFFER, ACK and NAK are server messages. On an untrusted port they can only come from a rogue server, so the switch always discards them.

sections.title: Configuring and verifying DHCP snooping
sections.body:
Two global commands are both required: `ip dhcp snooping` turns the feature on, and `ip dhcp snooping vlan 10` chooses the VLANs (a list such as `10,20` also works). Then mark the ports toward the real server as trusted with the interface command `ip dhcp snooping trust`. Every other port stays untrusted by default.

Two details trip people up. First, by default the switch inserts **DHCP option 82** (relay agent information) into client requests, as if it were a relay agent. On a plain Layer 2 access switch that is not a relay, most servers and relays then discard those requests, so `no ip dhcp snooping information option` is usually needed. Second, snooping runs on the switch CPU, so an attacker can try to overwhelm it. `ip dhcp snooping limit rate 10` on an interface err-disables the port if more than 10 DHCP messages arrive in a second. There is no limit by default, the limit can be set on trusted or untrusted ports, and `errdisable recovery cause dhcp-rate-limit` makes the shutdown self-healing.

Verify with `show ip dhcp snooping`. It confirms the feature is enabled, lists the VLANs where snooping is configured and where it is operational, shows the option 82 setting, and lists only the interfaces that have a non-default trust or rate setting, so a port missing from that list is an untrusted port with no limit. `show ip dhcp snooping binding` lists the bindings, and `show ip dhcp snooping statistics` counts what was dropped. Do not confuse the binding table with `show ip dhcp binding`, which is the lease list on a router acting as the DHCP server.
sections.code:
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
SW1(config)# no ip dhcp snooping information option
SW1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust
SW1(config-if)# interface range GigabitEthernet0/1 - 23
SW1(config-if-range)# ip dhcp snooping limit rate 10

SW1# show ip dhcp snooping
Switch DHCP snooping is enabled
DHCP snooping is configured on following VLANs:
10
DHCP snooping is operational on following VLANs:
10
! lines omitted
Insertion of option 82 is disabled
! lines omitted
DHCP snooping trust/rate is configured on the following Interfaces:

Interface                  Trusted    Allow option    Rate limit (pps)
-----------------------    -------    ------------    ----------------
GigabitEthernet0/1         no         no              10
! lines omitted
GigabitEthernet0/24        yes        yes             unlimited
sections.pitfall: Enabling DHCP snooping and forgetting to trust the uplink toward the real server. Every legitimate OFFER and ACK then arrives on an untrusted port and is dropped, and no client gets an address.

check.question: Which command lists the MAC address, IP address, lease time, VLAN and interface that the switch learned for each DHCP client?
choices: show ip dhcp binding
show ip dhcp snooping binding
show mac address-table dynamic
show ip arp inspection
check.explanation: The snooping binding table lives on the switch and is shown with show ip dhcp snooping binding. show ip dhcp binding shows the leases of an IOS DHCP server, which may be a different device.

sections.title: Dynamic ARP Inspection
sections.body:
DHCP snooping stops the rogue server, but an attacker with a perfectly valid lease can still send forged ARP replies saying "10.1.10.1 is at my MAC" and pull the gateway's traffic through itself. ARP has no authentication, and hosts even accept a **gratuitous ARP**: a reply nobody asked for, sent to the broadcast address. **Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)** closes that hole.

With DAI enabled on a VLAN, the switch intercepts every ARP message (requests and replies) that arrives on an **untrusted** port and compares the sender MAC and sender IP inside the ARP message with the **DHCP snooping binding table** and any configured ARP ACLs. If the pair matches, the ARP is forwarded. If not, it is dropped and logged. Requests are checked as well as replies, because an ARP request also teaches every receiver the sender's IP and MAC. ARP messages on **trusted** ports are not checked; trust the same uplinks you trusted for DHCP snooping, plus any link to another switch or a router.

That dependency sets the configuration order: run DHCP snooping first so the binding table exists, then enable DAI with `ip arp inspection vlan 10` and trust the uplinks with `ip arp inspection trust`. If you enable DAI without DHCP snooping or ARP ACLs, every ARP on untrusted ports in that VLAN is dropped, and hosts lose connectivity as their ARP caches expire. Hosts with static addresses need special handling, covered in the next section.

`show ip arp inspection interfaces` shows each port's trust state and rate limit, as in the output below.
sections.code:
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection vlan 10
SW1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# ip arp inspection trust

SW1# show ip arp inspection interfaces
 Interface        Trust State     Rate (pps)    Burst Interval
 ---------------  -----------     ----------    --------------
 Gi0/1            Untrusted               15                 1
 Gi0/2            Untrusted               15                 1
 Gi0/24           Trusted               None               N/A

%SW_DAI-4-DHCP_SNOOPING_DENY: 1 Invalid ARPs (Res) on Gi0/2, vlan 10.
([0200.6666.6666/10.1.10.1/0200.1111.1111/10.1.10.101/...])

activity.title: DHCP snooping and DAI
activity.prompt: Protect VLAN 10: enable DHCP snooping globally and for the VLAN, trust the uplink G0/24, then enable Dynamic ARP Inspection for VLAN 10 and trust G0/24 for ARP as well. Before you start, predict what would break if you trusted nothing. When done, compare show ip dhcp snooping with show ip arp inspection.

sections.pitfall: Enabling DAI without trusting the uplink. The router's ARP replies arrive on an untrusted port, and the router has a static address with no snooping binding, so they are dropped and the whole VLAN loses its default gateway.

check.question: Dynamic ARP Inspection decides whether an ARP message on an untrusted port is legitimate by checking it against what?
choices: The switch's MAC address table
The DHCP snooping binding table
The router's routing table
The port security sticky addresses
check.explanation: DAI compares the sender MAC and IP in the ARP message with the bindings DHCP snooping learned (or an ARP ACL for static hosts). That is why DHCP snooping is configured first.

sections.title: DAI in practice: static hosts, extra checks and rate limits
sections.body:
Three practical details decide whether DAI helps or hurts.

**Static hosts.** Servers, printers and routers with manually configured addresses never use DHCP, so they have no snooping binding, and DAI drops their ARP messages on untrusted ports. Either trust the port (fine for a router or another switch, not for an end host), or describe the host in an **ARP ACL** and apply it to the VLAN with `ip arp inspection filter`. DAI checks ARP ACLs as well as the binding table.

**Extra checks.** `ip arp inspection validate` adds optional tests on top of the core check: `src-mac` drops ARPs whose Ethernet source MAC differs from the sender MAC inside the ARP message, `dst-mac` does the same for the destination MAC of ARP replies, and `ip` drops ARPs carrying invalid addresses such as 0.0.0.0, 255.255.255.255 or multicast. Put every option you want in one command, because a new `validate` command replaces the previous one.

**Rate limits.** DAI also runs on the switch CPU, so it limits ARP by default: **15 ARP messages per second** on each untrusted port. Exceed it and the port is err-disabled. Raise it on busy ports with `ip arp inspection limit rate 25` (optionally with `burst interval 4` to measure over 4 seconds), and recover automatically with `errdisable recovery cause arp-inspection`.

To verify, `show ip arp inspection` shows the validation settings and per-VLAN counters, `show ip arp inspection statistics` shows the counters alone, and the log names every dropped ARP. In the counters, **DHCP Drops** are ARPs that matched no snooping binding, and **ACL Drops** are ARPs denied by an ARP ACL.
sections.code:
arp access-list STATIC-HOSTS
 permit ip host 10.1.10.50 mac host 0200.5050.5050
!
ip arp inspection filter STATIC-HOSTS vlan 10
ip arp inspection validate src-mac dst-mac ip
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip arp inspection limit rate 25

SW1# show ip arp inspection statistics vlan 10
 Vlan      Forwarded        Dropped     DHCP Drops      ACL Drops
 ----      ---------        -------     ----------      ---------
   10           5214             17             17              0
sections.pitfall: Turning on DAI in a VLAN that contains statically addressed servers or printers without an ARP ACL. They have no snooping bindings, so every ARP they send is dropped and they vanish from the network.

check.question: A PC on Gi0/4 has been statically configured with 10.1.10.101, an address DHCP already leased to another PC on Gi0/3. DAI is enabled on the VLAN. What happens to the ARPs from the PC on Gi0/4?
choices: They are forwarded, because static hosts are exempt from DAI
They are dropped, because their sender MAC and IP pair matches no binding
Gi0/3 is err-disabled
The binding table is updated with the new MAC
check.explanation: The binding for 10.1.10.101 lists the first PC's MAC on Gi0/3. The ARP from Gi0/4 claims that IP with a different MAC, so DAI drops it and logs a DHCP snooping deny. That is exactly what stops an attacker from claiming someone else's address.

sections.title: Hardening the rest of the access port
sections.body:
Port security, DHCP snooping and DAI protect ports that are in use. The rest of the access layer needs attention too, and Cisco's recommendations are short.

- **Unused ports**: `shutdown`, make them access ports with `switchport mode access`, and assign them to an unused VLAN that goes nowhere. Shutting them down removes the exposure; the other two steps keep the port safe if someone later types `no shutdown`.
- **No trunk negotiation on user ports**: configure `switchport mode access`, and use `switchport nonegotiate` on trunks that do not need DTP. A port left in dynamic desirable or dynamic auto lets an attacker's device negotiate a trunk with DTP and reach every VLAN, an attack called **switch spoofing**.
- **Native VLAN**: on trunks, set the native VLAN to an unused VLAN rather than VLAN 1, and never put users in it. In a **double-tagging** attack, a host in the native VLAN sends a frame with two 802.1Q tags. The first switch removes the outer tag, because native VLAN frames cross the trunk untagged, and the next switch reads the inner tag and delivers the frame into the victim's VLAN. It only works one way, but it crosses a VLAN boundary without a router.
- **Spanning tree protection**: BPDU Guard on access ports err-disables a port that receives BPDUs, so nobody can plug in a switch and try to become the root bridge. The STP pack covers it along with Root Guard, Loop Guard and BPDU Filter.

Together with port security, DHCP snooping, DAI and the 802.1X authentication in the next section, these settings turn an access port from "anything plugged in gets a VLAN" into "only known devices, with known addresses, get exactly what they need."
sections.code:
! Unused ports: access mode, parked in an unused VLAN, shut down
interface range GigabitEthernet0/13 - 22
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 999
 shutdown
!
! User ports: never negotiate a trunk, reject BPDUs
interface range GigabitEthernet0/1 - 12
 switchport mode access
 spanning-tree bpduguard enable
!
! Uplink: fixed trunk, no DTP, unused native VLAN
interface GigabitEthernet0/24
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport nonegotiate
 switchport trunk native vlan 998
sections.pitfall: Leaving user ports in a dynamic DTP mode. dynamic auto looks harmless, but any device that sends DTP desirable messages turns the port into a trunk that carries every VLAN.

check.question: Why should a trunk's native VLAN be an unused VLAN rather than VLAN 1 or a user VLAN?
choices: It makes the trunk faster
It stops hosts from using double-tagged frames to reach other VLANs through the native VLAN
It is required for DTP to work
It encrypts untagged frames on the trunk
check.explanation: Double tagging relies on the attacker sitting in the trunk's native VLAN. If no host is in that VLAN, the outer tag can never match it, and the attack fails.

sections.title: 802.1X: authenticating devices before the port opens
sections.body:
Port security trusts a MAC address, and MAC addresses are easy to copy. **IEEE 802.1X** goes further: the port refuses all normal traffic until the device or user proves who it is to a central server. It is the same framework that WPA2 and WPA3 Enterprise use on Wi-Fi, applied here to wired switch ports.

Three roles take part:

- The **supplicant** is the software on the PC that answers with credentials, such as a certificate or a username and password.
- The **authenticator** is the access switch. It does not judge the credentials; it relays them and controls the port.
- The **authentication server** is a RADIUS server such as Cisco ISE, which makes the decision.

Between the PC and the switch, the credentials travel in **EAP over LAN (EAPoL)** frames. Between the switch and the server, the same EAP messages ride inside **RADIUS** (UDP 1812). Until the server answers with an Access-Accept, the port is in the **unauthorized** state and passes only EAPoL, so the PC cannot even get a DHCP address. After an accept the port is authorized, and the server can also tell the switch which VLAN or ACL to apply to that user, which is AAA authorization in action.

Devices that have no supplicant, such as printers and IP cameras, can fall back to **MAC Authentication Bypass (MAB)**, where the switch sends the device's MAC address to the server as its identity. The configuration below shows the IOS building blocks: AAA turned on, a RADIUS server, 802.1X enabled globally and the port set to `authentication port-control auto`.
sections.code:
aaa new-model
radius server ISE1
 address ipv4 10.10.99.20 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813
 key R@diusKey!24
aaa authentication dot1x default group radius
dot1x system-auth-control
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/5
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 authentication port-control auto
 dot1x pae authenticator

PC (supplicant) --EAPoL--> SW1 (authenticator) --RADIUS, UDP 1812--> ISE (authentication server)
sections.pitfall: Thinking the switch checks the user's password. The switch is only the authenticator; it relays EAP to the RADIUS server, which makes the decision.

check.question: Before 802.1X authentication succeeds on a port configured with authentication port-control auto, which traffic does the switch accept from the PC?
choices: DHCP and DNS only
All traffic in the access VLAN
Only EAPoL frames
Only traffic addressed to the RADIUS server
check.explanation: An unauthorized 802.1X port passes only EAPoL, which carries the authentication exchange. Everything else, DHCP included, waits until the RADIUS server accepts the device.

keyTerms.definition: An attack that fills a switch's MAC table with fake source addresses so frames are flooded out every port.
A switch port feature that limits how many and which source MAC addresses may use the port.
A dynamically learned secure MAC that port security writes into the running configuration.
What port security does on a violation: protect (drop silently), restrict (drop, log, count) or shutdown (err-disable the port).
A state in which the switch has disabled a port because of an error or security violation; recover with shutdown and no shutdown or errdisable recovery.
A switch feature that drops DHCP server messages on untrusted ports, checks client messages and builds a binding table.
A port facing infrastructure (uplink, router, real DHCP server) where DHCP snooping and DAI do not filter messages.
The switch's record of each client's MAC, leased IP, lease time, VLAN and interface.
DHCP relay agent information that a snooping switch inserts by default; usually disabled on Layer 2 switches that are not relay agents.
A switch feature that drops ARP messages on untrusted ports whose MAC and IP do not match the DHCP snooping bindings.
An ARP reply sent without a request, to the broadcast address; legitimate for address changes, abused for ARP poisoning.
A list of permitted IP and MAC pairs that DAI checks for hosts with static addresses.
An attack where a device negotiates a trunk with DTP to reach every VLAN; prevented by static access ports.
A one-way VLAN hopping attack using two 802.1Q tags from a host in the trunk's native VLAN.
Port-based access control that admits a device only after a RADIUS server authenticates it through EAP.
EAP over LAN: the frames that carry 802.1X authentication between the supplicant and the switch.

summary: Access-edge attacks (MAC flooding, rogue DHCP, starvation, ARP poisoning, VLAN hopping) happen inside the LAN, so the defenses live on the access switch.
Port security needs a static access or trunk port; the defaults are a maximum of 1 MAC and shutdown mode; sticky MACs go into the running config, so save it.
protect drops silently, restrict drops, logs and counts, shutdown err-disables; recover with shutdown and no shutdown or errdisable recovery.
DHCP snooping trusts uplinks, drops OFFER, ACK and NAK on untrusted ports, checks chaddr and RELEASE messages, and builds the binding table; disable option 82 on Layer 2 switches.
DAI checks ARP on untrusted ports against the snooping bindings and ARP ACLs, limits untrusted ports to 15 ARPs per second, and can validate MAC and IP fields.
Shut and park unused ports, never let user ports negotiate trunks, use an unused native VLAN, and use 802.1X (with MAB for simple devices) to authenticate before the port opens.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a junior technician how an attacker on a conference room jack could become a man in the middle using a rogue DHCP server or ARP poisoning, or reach other VLANs through DTP, and how DHCP snooping, Dynamic ARP Inspection, port security, static access ports and 802.1X together stop each step.

questions.question: An attack tool sends thousands of frames per second, each with a different made-up source MAC address. What is this attack, and which feature limits it?
choices: ARP poisoning, stopped by DHCP snooping
MAC flooding, limited by port security
DHCP starvation, stopped by DAI
VLAN hopping, stopped by BPDU guard
questions.explanation: Inventing source MACs to fill the MAC table is MAC flooding. Port security caps how many MACs each port may introduce.

questions.question: Match each attack to the switch feature designed to stop it.

pairs.left: Unauthorized laptop on a desk port
Rogue DHCP server handing out a fake gateway
Forged ARP replies claiming the gateway's IP
Thousands of fake source MACs filling the MAC table

questions.explanation: Port security controls MACs per port, DHCP snooping filters DHCP server messages on untrusted ports, and DAI validates ARP against the snooping bindings.

questions.question: An attacker sends DHCP Discover messages, each with a different invented client hardware address, until the server's pool runs out. What is this attack called?
choices: DHCP starvation
DHCP spoofing
MAC flooding
ARP poisoning
questions.explanation: Exhausting the server's address pool with fake requests is DHCP starvation. It is often followed by a rogue DHCP server that answers clients the real server can no longer serve.

questions.question: What is the default violation mode for port security?
choices: protect
restrict
log
shutdown
questions.explanation: By default a violation err-disables the port (shutdown mode). protect and restrict must be configured explicitly.

questions.question: An engineer sees the message below. What must be done before port security can be enabled on Gi0/5?
questions.code:
SW1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/5
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security
Command rejected: GigabitEthernet0/5 is a dynamic port.
choices: Set the port statically to access (or trunk) mode, for example with switchport mode access
Enable port security globally first
Shut the port down first
Configure a sticky MAC address first
questions.explanation: Port security requires a port that is statically an access or trunk port. A port left in dynamic auto or desirable mode is rejected.

questions.question: Match each kind of secure MAC address to how it behaves.

pairs.right: Typed by the administrator with the MAC address
Learned from traffic and lost when the switch reloads
Learned from traffic and written into the running configuration

questions.explanation: Sticky combines the convenience of learning with the persistence of configuration, provided the running configuration is saved.

questions.question: An access port connects an IP phone with a PC plugged into the phone. Port security is enabled with default settings, and the port keeps going err-disabled. What change is appropriate?
choices: Change the violation mode to protect
Disable sticky learning
Raise the maximum to 2 so both the phone and the PC are allowed
Convert the port to a trunk
questions.explanation: The default maximum of 1 allows only one MAC, but the phone and the PC each have their own. Allowing two keeps security while letting both work. protect would just make the PC fail silently.

questions.question: Which two statements about sticky secure MAC addresses are true? (Choose two.)
choices: They are learned dynamically and added to the running configuration
They survive a reload only if the running configuration is saved to startup
They are written to the startup configuration automatically
They must be typed manually by the administrator
They age out of the table after five minutes by default
questions.explanation: Sticky addresses are learned, then written into the running configuration. Like any running-config change, they are lost on reload unless saved with copy running-config startup-config.

questions.question: Port Gi0/7 has the configuration below, yet a second laptop plugged into a hub on that port works without any violation. Why?
questions.code:
interface GigabitEthernet0/7
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 20
 switchport port-security maximum 1
 switchport port-security violation shutdown
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky
!
SW1# show port-security interface Gi0/7 | include Port Security
Port Security              : Disabled
choices: The violation mode must be restrict for hubs
Sticky learning overrides the maximum
VLAN 20 is exempt from port security
The switchport port-security command that actually enables the feature is missing
questions.explanation: IOS stores the maximum, violation and sticky settings, but port security stays disabled until the plain switchport port-security command is entered on the interface.

questions.question: You are in interface configuration mode on a static access port. Type the command that enables port security on it.
questions.explanation: switchport port-security turns the feature on with its defaults: a maximum of 1 MAC and the shutdown violation mode.

questions.question: Type the interface command that makes port security learn the connected device's MAC address and save it in the running configuration.
questions.explanation: Sticky learning writes each learned secure MAC into the running configuration, so it can be saved and survive a reload.

questions.question: Type the interface command that allows up to 3 secure MAC addresses on a port.
questions.explanation: maximum overrides the default of 1. A fourth source MAC would then be a violation.

questions.question: Based on the output below, which statement is true?
questions.code:
SW1# show port-security interface GigabitEthernet0/2
Port Security              : Enabled
Port Status                : Secure-up
Violation Mode             : Shutdown
Maximum MAC Addresses      : 1
Total MAC Addresses        : 1
Configured MAC Addresses   : 1
Sticky MAC Addresses       : 1
Last Source Address:Vlan   : 0200.2222.2222:10
Security Violation Count   : 0
choices: The port is err-disabled after a violation
The port learned 0200.2222.2222 as a sticky address and is forwarding normally
The MAC address was typed statically by the administrator
Port security is configured but not active
questions.explanation: Secure-up with zero violations means the port is forwarding normally. Sticky MAC Addresses: 1 shows the address was learned with sticky learning; a sticky address is also counted as configured because it was written into the running configuration, so the Configured field alone cannot tell you it was typed by hand.

questions.question: A port uses sticky learning. The switch reloads before anyone saves the configuration. What happens?
choices: The sticky MAC is restored from the MAC address table
The port refuses all devices until a MAC is configured
The sticky MAC is lost, and the port learns the first MAC it sees after the reload
The port is err-disabled at boot
questions.explanation: Sticky addresses are in the running configuration only. Without copy running-config startup-config, the reload discards them and learning starts over.

questions.question: Match each port security violation mode to its behavior.

pairs.right: Drops violating frames silently; no log, no counter
Drops violating frames, logs them and increments the counter; port stays up
Puts the port in the err-disabled state

questions.explanation: All three discard offending traffic. restrict adds visibility, and shutdown stops the whole port.

questions.question: A user reports the network is dead at their desk. What do these outputs show?
questions.code:
SW1# show interfaces Gi0/13 status
Port      Name    Status        Vlan   Duplex  Speed  Type
Gi0/13            err-disabled  10     auto    auto   10/100/1000BaseTX

SW1# show port-security interface Gi0/13
Port Security              : Enabled
Port Status                : Secure-shutdown
Violation Mode             : Shutdown
Maximum MAC Addresses      : 1
Total MAC Addresses        : 1
Last Source Address:Vlan   : 0200.3333.3333:10
Security Violation Count   : 1
choices: A port security violation from MAC 0200.3333.3333 err-disabled the port
The cable is faulty, so the port is down/down
The port was shut down by an administrator
DHCP snooping rate limiting disabled the port
questions.explanation: err-disabled plus Secure-shutdown and a violation count of 1 point to a port security violation in shutdown mode. The last source address shows the device that caused it.

questions.question: Port Gi0/13 shows the output below and stays up, yet one device behind it cannot communicate. What is happening?
questions.code:
SW1# show port-security interface Gi0/13
Port Security              : Enabled
Port Status                : Secure-up
Violation Mode             : Restrict
Maximum MAC Addresses      : 1
Total MAC Addresses        : 1
Configured MAC Addresses   : 1
Last Source Address:Vlan   : 0200.3333.3333:10
Security Violation Count   : 97
choices: The port is err-disabled but the status has not refreshed
Port security is in protect mode and is counting silently
The allowed device is sending too many frames
Frames from 0200.3333.3333 exceed the one allowed MAC and are being dropped and counted, while the configured MAC still works
questions.explanation: In restrict mode the port stays Secure-up for the allowed MAC and drops frames from extra MACs, counting each one. 97 dropped frames from 0200.3333.3333 explain the failing device.

questions.question: A port was err-disabled by a port security violation. Put the manual recovery steps in order.
items: Identify the violating device from the log or show port-security interface
Remove the unauthorized device or fix the configuration
Enter no shutdown on the interface
Confirm the port shows Secure-up and the user is connected
questions.explanation: Removing the cause comes before bouncing the port; otherwise the next frame from the device err-disables the port again.

questions.question: Type the global command that lets the switch automatically recover ports that were err-disabled by port security violations.
questions.explanation: errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation enables auto-recovery for this cause; errdisable recovery interval sets how long the switch waits (300 seconds by default).

questions.question: A port shows Secure-up and a violation count of 0, but a second PC on a small hub behind the port cannot reach anything. No syslog messages appear. Which violation mode is most likely configured?
choices: shutdown
restrict
protect
sticky
questions.explanation: protect drops violating frames without logging or counting, so the port looks healthy. restrict would show a rising counter, and shutdown would err-disable the port. Sticky is a learning method, not a mode.

questions.question: With DHCP snooping, which switch port should be configured as trusted?
choices: Every access port that has a PC
The uplink toward the legitimate DHCP server or relay
Ports connected to wireless guests
Unused ports
questions.explanation: Only ports facing the real DHCP server (or the router relaying to it) should be trusted. Client-facing ports stay untrusted, the default.

questions.question: Which two DHCP messages are always dropped when they arrive on a DHCP snooping untrusted port? (Choose two.)
choices: DHCPOFFER
DHCPACK
DHCPDISCOVER
DHCPREQUEST
DHCPRELEASE from the interface in the binding table
questions.explanation: OFFER and ACK (and NAK) are server messages, which should never come from a client port. DISCOVER and REQUEST are client messages that are checked, not automatically dropped.

questions.question: Which two global commands are both required to turn on DHCP snooping for VLAN 10? (Choose two.)
choices: ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
ip dhcp snooping trust
no ip dhcp snooping information option
ip arp inspection vlan 10
questions.explanation: Snooping must be enabled globally and for each VLAN. trust is an interface command, the option 82 command is optional, and ip arp inspection is a separate feature.

questions.question: You are in interface configuration mode on the uplink to the DHCP server. Type the command that makes it a DHCP snooping trusted port.
questions.explanation: Ports are untrusted by default. ip dhcp snooping trust allows server messages such as OFFER and ACK through this port.

questions.question: On a Layer 2 access switch (not a DHCP relay), DHCP snooping is enabled for VLAN 10 and the uplink is trusted. Clients still get no addresses, and the DHCP server logs show it is discarding their requests. What is the most likely fix?
questions.code:
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/24
 ip dhcp snooping trust
choices: Trust all access ports as well
Remove the trust from the uplink
Add no ip dhcp snooping information option, so the switch stops inserting option 82
Add ip dhcp snooping limit rate 1 on the uplink
questions.explanation: By default the snooping switch inserts option 82 into client requests, and many servers and relays discard requests carrying it from a switch that is not a relay agent. Disabling the insertion fixes it.

questions.question: How does DHCP snooping defeat a starvation tool that sends many Discovers from one laptop, each with a different invented client hardware address?
choices: It checks that the Ethernet source MAC matches the chaddr inside each DHCP message
It drops every DISCOVER on untrusted ports
It forwards Discovers only to the rogue server
It converts the port to a trunk
questions.explanation: On untrusted ports, DISCOVER and REQUEST messages must have a chaddr equal to the frame's source MAC. The tool's frames all carry the laptop's real MAC, so the mismatched requests are dropped.

questions.question: What information does the DHCP snooping binding table hold for each client?
questions.code:
SW1# show ip dhcp snooping binding
MacAddress          IpAddress        Lease(sec)  Type           VLAN  Interface
02:00:11:11:11:11   10.1.10.101      86110       dhcp-snooping   10   GigabitEthernet0/3
choices: The client's hostname, gateway and DNS server
Only the client's MAC address and port
The DHCP server's address and pool name
The client's MAC, leased IP, lease time, VLAN and switch interface
questions.explanation: Each binding ties a MAC and IP to a VLAN and interface, with the remaining lease time. DAI and IP Source Guard check traffic against these bindings.

questions.question: An access port has ip dhcp snooping limit rate 10. A misbehaving host sends 50 DHCP messages in one second. What happens?
choices: The extra 40 messages are dropped and the port stays up
The port is err-disabled
The port becomes trusted automatically
Nothing, because rate limits apply only to trusted ports
questions.explanation: Exceeding the DHCP snooping rate limit err-disables the port. errdisable recovery cause dhcp-rate-limit can bring it back automatically.

questions.question: Which attack does Dynamic ARP Inspection prevent?
choices: MAC flooding
DHCP starvation
ARP spoofing (ARP poisoning)
VLAN hopping
questions.explanation: DAI drops ARP messages whose sender MAC and IP do not match the switch's DHCP snooping bindings, which stops forged ARP replies.

questions.question: Type the global command that enables Dynamic ARP Inspection for VLAN 10.
questions.explanation: DAI is enabled per VLAN. Uplinks are then marked trusted with the interface command ip arp inspection trust.

questions.question: After DHCP snooping and DAI are enabled on VLAN 10, every DHCP client works, but a network printer with a manually configured static IP can no longer be reached. Why, and what fixes it?
choices: The printer has no DHCP snooping binding, so DAI drops its ARPs; add an ARP ACL for it with ip arp inspection filter
Static IPs are not allowed in VLANs with DAI; move the printer to DHCP is the only option
The printer's port must be configured with port security
DAI only checks ARP requests, so the printer's replies are lost
questions.explanation: DAI validates against the snooping bindings, and a static host never creates one. An ARP ACL listing the printer's IP and MAC (applied with ip arp inspection filter) lets DAI accept its ARPs. Using DHCP reservations is another option, but not the only one.

questions.question: Put these steps in a sensible order to protect VLAN 10 with both DHCP snooping and DAI.
items: Enable DHCP snooping globally with ip dhcp snooping
Enable DHCP snooping for the VLAN with ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
Trust the uplink for DHCP with ip dhcp snooping trust
Enable DAI for the VLAN with ip arp inspection vlan 10
Trust the uplink for ARP with ip arp inspection trust
questions.explanation: DAI depends on the binding table that DHCP snooping builds, so snooping comes first. Each feature has its own trust command on the uplink.

questions.question: Based on the output below, what happens if a host on Gi0/1 sends 40 ARP packets in one second?
questions.code:
SW1# show ip arp inspection interfaces
 Interface        Trust State     Rate (pps)    Burst Interval
 ---------------  -----------     ----------    --------------
 Gi0/1            Untrusted               15                 1
 Gi0/24           Trusted               None               N/A
choices: The extra ARPs are queued until the next second
Nothing, because ARP is never rate-limited
Gi0/1 is err-disabled for exceeding the DAI rate limit
Gi0/1 becomes a trusted port
questions.explanation: Untrusted ports are limited to 15 ARP packets per second by default. Exceeding it err-disables the port; errdisable recovery cause arp-inspection can recover it automatically.

questions.question: Why must DHCP snooping be configured before (or along with) Dynamic ARP Inspection?
questions.answer: DAI decides whether an ARP message is legitimate by comparing its sender MAC and IP with the DHCP snooping binding table. Without snooping there are no bindings, so DAI would drop every ARP on untrusted ports in the VLAN (except hosts covered by an ARP ACL).
questions.explanation: The two features work as a pair: snooping learns who legitimately owns each address, and DAI enforces it for ARP.

questions.question: PC1 leased 10.1.10.101 through Gi0/3, and DHCP snooping is enabled. An attacker on Gi0/5 sends a DHCPRELEASE for 10.1.10.101. What happens?
choices: The switch forwards it and the server frees the address
The switch drops it, because the binding table shows the address was leased on Gi0/3
The switch err-disables Gi0/3
The switch makes Gi0/5 trusted
questions.explanation: RELEASE and DECLINE messages on untrusted ports must arrive on the interface in the address's binding. This stops an attacker from releasing a victim's lease and then requesting the same address.

questions.question: After DHCP snooping was enabled, no client in VLAN 10 gets an address. The DHCP server is reached through uplink Gi0/24. Based on the output, what is the cause?
questions.code:
SW1# show ip dhcp snooping
Switch DHCP snooping is enabled
DHCP snooping is configured on following VLANs:
10
DHCP snooping is operational on following VLANs:
10
! lines omitted
Insertion of option 82 is disabled
! lines omitted
DHCP snooping trust/rate is configured on the following Interfaces:

Interface                  Trusted    Allow option    Rate limit (pps)
-----------------------    -------    ------------    ----------------
GigabitEthernet0/1         no         no              10
choices: Option 82 insertion is disabled
The rate limit on Gi0/1 is too low
Gi0/24 is not trusted, so the server's OFFER and ACK messages are dropped
DHCP snooping is not operational on VLAN 10
questions.explanation: The interface list shows only ports with a non-default trust or rate setting. Gi0/24 is missing, so it is untrusted, and server messages arriving on it are discarded. Disabling option 82 is correct for a Layer 2 switch, and snooping is operational on VLAN 10.

questions.question: What do these outputs show?
questions.code:
SW1# show ip arp inspection statistics vlan 10
 Vlan      Forwarded        Dropped     DHCP Drops      ACL Drops
 ----      ---------        -------     ----------      ---------
   10           5214             17             17              0
SW1# show logging | include DAI
%SW_DAI-4-DHCP_SNOOPING_DENY: 1 Invalid ARPs (Req) on Gi0/4, vlan 10.([0200.2222.2222/10.1.10.101/0000.0000.0000/10.1.10.1/09:28:20 UTC Thu Jul 25 2024])
choices: DAI dropped 17 ARPs that matched no snooping binding, including one from Gi0/4 claiming 10.1.10.101 with MAC 0200.2222.2222
An ARP ACL denied 17 ARPs on Gi0/4
Gi0/4 exceeded the ARP rate limit and was err-disabled
The DHCP server on Gi0/4 has run out of addresses
questions.explanation: DHCP Drops counts ARPs whose sender MAC and IP pair is not in the binding table; ACL Drops is zero. The log shows the offending sender MAC and IP, which belong to a host trying to use an address leased to someone else.

questions.question: Type the global command that makes DAI also drop ARP messages whose Ethernet source MAC differs from the sender MAC inside the ARP message.
questions.explanation: ip arp inspection validate adds optional checks: src-mac, dst-mac and ip. Enter all the options you want in one command, because a new validate command replaces the old one.

questions.question: Which three settings does Cisco recommend for unused switch ports? (Choose three.)
choices: shutdown
switchport mode access
Assign the port to an unused VLAN
switchport mode dynamic desirable
Leave the port in VLAN 1
questions.explanation: Shutting the port down removes the exposure, access mode prevents trunk negotiation, and an unused VLAN limits the damage if the port is ever enabled. Dynamic desirable invites a trunk, and VLAN 1 is the default everyone expects.

questions.question: VLAN 1 is the native VLAN on the trunk between SW1 and SW2. A host in VLAN 1 on SW1 sends a frame with two 802.1Q tags: outer VLAN 1, inner VLAN 20. What can happen?
choices: SW1 drops every double-tagged frame by default
SW1 removes the outer tag and sends the frame across the trunk with the inner tag, so SW2 delivers it into VLAN 20
The frame reaches VLAN 20 and replies come back to the attacker the same way
SW2 rewrites the frame into VLAN 1
questions.explanation: Native VLAN frames cross the trunk untagged, so SW1 strips the matching outer tag and leaves the inner one, which SW2 obeys. Replies cannot come back the same way, so the attack is one-way. Using an unused native VLAN prevents it.

questions.question: A user port was left in switchport mode dynamic desirable, and an attacker's laptop runs a tool that speaks DTP. What is the risk, and what is the fix?
choices: The laptop can negotiate a trunk and reach every VLAN; configure switchport mode access
The laptop can become the STP root; enable PortFast
The laptop can exhaust the DHCP pool; enable DAI
There is no risk; DTP only forms trunks between two Cisco switches
questions.explanation: This is switch spoofing: the laptop answers DTP and the port becomes a trunk carrying all VLANs. A static access port never negotiates a trunk.

questions.question: Match each 802.1X term to its role on a wired network.

pairs.right: Software on the user's PC that provides credentials
The access switch that relays EAP and controls the port
The RADIUS server, such as Cisco ISE, that decides
How EAP travels between the PC and the switch

questions.explanation: The switch never judges credentials; it carries EAP from the PC (in EAPoL frames) to the server (inside RADIUS) and opens the port when the server accepts.

questions.question: You are configuring an access port for 802.1X. Type the interface command that makes the port require authentication before it forwards normal traffic.
questions.explanation: authentication port-control auto starts the port unauthorized and opens it only after the RADIUS server accepts the device. Older IOS releases used dot1x port-control auto.

questions.question: A network printer on an 802.1X-protected port has no supplicant software. Which feature lets the switch admit it, using its MAC address as its identity with the RADIUS server?
choices: Port security sticky learning
DHCP snooping
MAC Authentication Bypass (MAB)
BPDU Guard
questions.explanation: MAB sends the device's MAC address to the RADIUS server in place of EAP credentials, so the server still makes the decision. Sticky learning is local port security with no server involved.
